rationale: A wins because it knows where the floorboards are weak and labels them instead of tap-dancing over them. Its best tell is the proof demand: "how many of the 12,000 connected institutions actually support FedNow specifically (not all do)" — that is exactly the trap a real reporter would spring. B has useful shapes, but it keeps writing checks the update cannot cash: "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" and "Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes" are not supplied facts; they are confidence wearing a press badge.
gaps_in_A: "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" asserts a historical premise the update does not supply. A partially saves itself by asking for proof, but the headline still states the unproven thing.
"FedNow policy/infrastructure-adoption angle... duplicate" is too dismissive. A FedNow-commercial-adoption story can be structurally distinct if framed around the rail, not Plaid.

"retail payments" slightly over-broadens the update. The facts say merchants accepting account-to-account payments; the set should be careful not to imply consumer retail adoption without merchant examples.
gaps_in_B: "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" is an overclaim with no supplied basis. Significant compared with what? Says who? This is how a decent angle becomes a correction risk.
"Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes" imports Plaid history not given in the update. Maybe true, maybe not; in this exercise, it is still ungrounded decoration.
"competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen" invents a competitive frame the update does not provide. Useful question, bad asserted angle.

"Merchants using Plaid's Pay by Bank report fees up to 70% lower" subtly launders Plaid's claim into merchant testimony. The update says Plaid says early merchants see it; no named merchant has gone on record.
